en: Sutta Nipāta 5.5 Mettagūmāṇavapucchā “I ask you, Blessed One; tell me this:”
(Thus spoke the Venerable Mettagū:
"I consider you to be one who has attained knowledge and developed his self;
from where, indeed, have these sufferings arisen?"
"Whatever various forms there are in the world"—
"You are indeed asking me about the origin of suffering," said the Blessed One to Mettagū.
I shall declare that to you as I understand it:
whatever various kinds of suffering arise in the world, they all originate from the source of acquisitions (upadhi).
The fool who, being ignorant, creates acquisitions,
repeatedly encounters suffering;
therefore, one who understands should not create acquisitions.
“Beholding the origin of suffering as its source.
“That which we asked you, you have explained to us;
now we ask another, please tell us that.”
How indeed do the wise cross over the flood,
as well as birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation?
O Sage, please explain this to me well.
"For this Dhamma is known to you.
"I shall proclaim the Dhamma to you," [said the Blessed One,] Mettagū.
That which is known in this very life, not based on tradition—
having understood this and practicing with mindfulness,
one crosses over attachment to the world.
“And I rejoice in that supreme Dhamma, O Great Seer;
having understood it, one should live mindfully.”

"Cross over the attachment to the world. "Whatever you perceive, Mettagū," said the Blessed One, "is not found within you. "I do not see anything in the world," said Mettagū, "that would cause me grief. "If you do not see anything in the world that would cause you grief," said the Blessed One, "then why do you grieve for those who are grieving? "I do not grieve for those who are grieving," said Mettagū, "for I am not one of them. "Since you do not grieve for those who are grieving," said the Blessed One, "you have indeed crossed over attachment to the world. "I have indeed crossed over attachment to the world," said Mettagū, "and I no longer yearn for existence anywhere. Above, below, across, and in between—
having dispelled both delight and settling in these,
consciousness shall not remain in existence.
Dwelling thus, mindful and diligent,
a bhikkhu who moves about having abandoned things cherished,
[will transcend] birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation.
“Right here, a wise person should abandon suffering.
“I delight in these words of the Great Seer,
so well-proclaimed by Gotama regarding the state beyond acquisitions.”
Truly, the Blessed One has abandoned suffering,
for this Dhamma is known by you.
Surely they too shall abandon suffering.
O Sage, you who would exhort one who stands firm—
I pay homage to you, O Naga, having approached you;
may the Blessed One likewise exhort me so that I may stand firm.
“The brahmin whom one should recognize as a possessor of true knowledge—
one who possesses nothing and is unattached to sensual existence—
has indeed crossed over this flood.”
Having crossed over, free from harshness and doubt,
the wise man who is a master of knowledge here,
having relinquished this attachment to becoming and non-becoming;
"Thus, free from craving, untroubled, and without hope,
he has crossed over birth and old age— this I declare.
This is the fourth inquiry of the youth Mettagū.
